chunks.text: 45-year-old male, Associate Professional or Technician, resident of Bedok, Singapore.
General anesthesia with endotracheal intubation and rapid sequence induction

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Good morning, Mr./Ms. [Name]. I'm Dr. [Name], the anesthesiologist who'll be taking care of you during your surgery today. I'd like to go over a few things to make sure we're all set for your laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Is that okay with you?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Yes, doctor. Thank you lah.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Great. Can you tell me a bit about why you're having this surgery? What symptoms have you been experiencing?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Sure. I've been having this sharp pain on the right side of my belly, especially after eating. The doctor said it's gallstones, and they want to remove the gallbladder laparoscopically.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Understood. Now, let's go through your medications. You're currently on amlodipine, metoprolol, atorvastatin, omeprazole, and you've stopped aspirin. Is that correct?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Yes, doctor. I take all those except the aspirin, which I stopped a week ago as instructed.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Good. Now, regarding allergies—your records say 'no known allergies,' but I always like to confirm directly. Do you have any allergies to medications, including antibiotics like penicillin?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Oh, actually, yes. When I was younger, I took penicillin for a infection and got a bad rash all over. So I think I'm allergic to that.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Thank you for sharing that. It's important we update your records to reflect your penicillin allergy. Have you had any other reactions to medications?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: No, just that one time with penicillin. Other antibiotics seem fine.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Excellent. Have you eaten or drunk anything since midnight? We need to ensure you're NPO for surgery.

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: No, doctor. I had water until 6 AM but nothing else. My wife made sure I followed the instructions.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Perfect. Have you had any previous surgeries or anesthesia? Any complications like nausea, breathing issues, or high blood pressure during recovery?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: I had my appendix out when I was a teenager. The anesthesia was fine then—no problems at all.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Great. Lastly, how are you managing with daily activities? Any shortness of breath, chest pain, or difficulty mobilizing due to your weight or other conditions?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: I can walk and do my usual things, but sometimes I get a bit breathless if I rush. My blood pressure has been controlled with the meds, and I take omeprazole for the acid reflux.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Thank you for all that information. We'll proceed with general anesthesia and rapid sequence induction as planned. Your penicillin allergy will be clearly documented. Any questions for me before we head to the operating room?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: No, doctor. Just want to make sure stopping the aspirin was the right call.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Absolutely. Stopping it a week prior reduces bleeding risk during surgery. We'll manage your pain post-op with other medications. All set then?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Yes, thank you. I'm ready.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: [08:00] induction propofol one hundred twenty milligrams, fentanyl fifty micrograms, succinylcholine one hundred milligrams

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: [08:02] hypotension, BP ninety over sixty, treated with bolus and phenylephrine ten micrograms

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: [08:05] 20-gauge IV placed in right antecubital fossa, 500 mL crystalloid bolused

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: [08:10] ET tube size seven point five, grade one view

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: [08:20] tachycardia, heart rate ninety, treated with fentanyl twenty five micrograms

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Hi there, how are you feeling now after the surgery?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Eh, still a bit tired one lah, but okay. Got some pain here, you know.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Can you tell me more about the pain? Where is it, and how bad is it on a scale of 1 to 10?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Mostly around the tummy area, like where they cut. Maybe 4 or 5? Not too bad, but there.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Any nausea or vomiting since waking up? You mentioned before you have GERD, so we’re keeping an eye on that.

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Yeah, a bit of nausea earlier, but not throwing up. My throat also sore, like something stuck there.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: The sore throat is probably from the tube we used during surgery. It should get better in a day or two. Breathing okay otherwise?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Breathing fine, just the throat pain. But I don’t remember anything about the surgery, very foggy one.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: That’s normal because of the anesthesia. We’ll monitor your blood pressure and sugars given your hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Any dizziness or shortness of breath?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: No dizziness, but moving around a bit uncomfortable because of the belly. BMI 32 also, so maybe harder to move?

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: We’ll get physio to help with mobility. For your GERD, avoid lying flat and take your meds as prescribed. Any other concerns?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: No, think that’s all. Thanks for checking on me.

45-year-old male from Bedok, Singapore, undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy for gallstones with post-prandial right upper quadrant pain.
History of controlled hypertension on amlodipine and metoprolol, with occasional exertional breathlessness but no chest pain.
Current medications: amlodipine 5mg daily, metoprolol 50mg daily, atorvastatin 20mg daily, omeprazole 20mg daily for acid reflux. Aspirin 75mg daily was discontinued one week prior to surgery.
Penicillin allergy with rash reaction reported.
NPO since midnight; last intake was water until 6 AM.
ASA-PS II: Mild systemic disease (controlled hypertension on amlodipine and metoprolol).
General anesthesia with endotracheal intubation and rapid sequence induction planned.
No complications during previous appendectomy anesthesia.

Intra-operatively, at 08:00, propofol 120mg, fentanyl 50mcg, and succinylcholine 100mg were administered. At 08:02, hypotension (BP 90/60) was treated with phenylephrine 10mcg. A 20-gauge IV was placed in the right antecubital fossa at 08:05, followed by 500mL crystalloid fluid. Endotracheal intubation was achieved with a 7.5mm tube and grade 1 view. At 08:20, tachycardia (HR 90) was managed with an additional 25mcg fentanyl.

High risk for post-operative nausea and vomiting (PONV) due to laparoscopic surgery, intra-operative opioid administration, and history of acid reflux. Risk of hemodynamic instability (hypotension or hypertension) due to intra-operative hypotension requiring vasopressor and chronic antihypertensive medications. Risk of post-operative respiratory complications (e.g., atelectasis, hypoxia) due to history of exertional breathlessness and general anesthesia.

Monitor closely for signs of post-operative nausea and vomiting, maintain hemodynamic stability with attention to blood pressure fluctuations, and ensure adequate respiratory function post-extubation. Consider antiemetic prophylaxis and continue current antihypertensive regimen as scheduled.
